text.p: Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp. said Thursday it will take dramatic steps to change its business and deal with a massive federal investigation that has rocked the largest U.S. for-profit hospital company.
Directly addressing two target areas of the probe, Columbia said it will sell its home healthcare division and change its laboratory billing procedures.

In response to questions about Medicare billing, the Nashville, Tenn.-based firm said it will widen disclosure of its Medicare cost reports, impose a new review system on Medicare coding procedures and adopt a comprehensive regulatory compliance programme.

Annual cash incentive pay for employees will also be ended. "Eliminating short-term cash incentive compensation will simply remove any appearance of pay being tied to short-term objectives," said Dr. Thomas Frist, the company's newly appointed chairman and chief executive.

The company also repeated that it will halt a controversial practice of selling interests in hospitals to physicians. "Such interests unintentionally may lead to the appearance of conflicts of interest," the company said in a statement.
The wide-ranging package of reforms fulfils a pledge made last week by Frist to federal authorities with an eye toward ending the investigation that has thrown Columbia into turmoil.

The four-month old investigation by several federal agencies led last month to raids on 33 company facilities in six states and seizures of cartloads of files pertaining to laboratory billing and home healthcare.

Three Columbia midlevel managers were indicted last week on fraud charges. Shareholders have filed at least 11 lawsuits against the firm and the attorneys general of Florida, Texas and Alabama are investigating the company.

Columbia's former chief executive and its president were ousted on July 24 by the board of directors, angry with their handling of the probe. Frist, formerly vice chairman, was named to replace CEO Richard Scott. On Monday, Jack Bovender, a close friend of Frist, replaced former President David Vandewater.
"We have already committed to cooperating with all governmental agencies, but we need to do more," Frist said in a statement outlining his reform plans.

Columbia said it hired the law firm of Latham & Watkins and the accounting firm Deloitte & Touche, giving both broad powers to examine company practices, recommend new policies and procedures and work with the government.
Several of the proposed changes may require regulatory approvals from federal, state or local authorities before being implemented, the company said.
"Management believes that it is too early to anticipate what effect such actions will have on the company's financial position or results of operations," Columbia said.
The company's stock was off 6.25 cents at $34.4375 on the New York Stock Exchange at midday.
